```{r}
#installing/loading all of the packages needed for the assignment

#install.packages("dplyr")
library("dplyr")
#install.packages("e1071")
library("e1071")
```

```{r}
#Create simple filtered table with only variables of interest and ID
set.seed(404)

filtered <- original %>%
  select(ID, CreditCard, Online, Personal.Loan)

training <- filtered %>%
  group_by(CreditCard, Online, Personal.Loan) %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 0.6) %>%
  ungroup()

validation <- filtered %>%
  anti_join(training, by = "ID")

#delete ID column from 3 non-original tables
training   <- training   %>% select(-ID)
validation <- validation %>% select(-ID)
filtered <- filtered %>% select(-ID)
```

```{r}
#double check training and validation split is roughly 60/40
nrow(training) / nrow(filtered)    # should be ~0.60
nrow(validation) / nrow(filtered)  # should be ~0.40

#checking proportions 
training   %>% count(CreditCard, Online, Personal.Loan) %>% mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
validation %>% count(CreditCard, Online, Personal.Loan) %>% mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
```

Assignment 3 - Part A
Create a pivot table for the training data with Online as a column variable, CC as a row variable, and Loan as a secondary row variable. The values inside the table should convey the count. In R use functions melt() and cast(), or function table().
```{r}

PivotPartA <- ftable(table(training$CreditCard, training$Personal.Loan, training$Online,
                      dnn = c("CC", "Loan", "Online")),
                row.vars = c("CC", "Loan"),
                col.vars = "Online")
PivotPartA
```

Assignment 3 - Part D (i-vi)
Compute the following quantities [P(A | B) means “the probability of A given B”]:
i. P(CC = 1 | Loan = 1)
ii. P(Online = 1 | Loan = 1)
iii. P(Loan = 1)
iv. P(CC = 1 | Loan = 0)
v. P(Online = 1 | Loan = 0)
vi. P(Loan = 0)
```{r}
#i. (85/286) = 29.7%
#ii. (174/286) = 60.8%
#iii. (286/2997) = 9.5%
#iv. (796/2711) = 29.4%
#v. (1615/2711) = 59.6%
#vi. (2711/2997) = 90.5%
```

Assignment 3 - Part E
Use the quantities computed above to compute the naive Bayes probability P(Loan = 1 | CC = 1, Online = 1).
```{r}
p1 <- ((85/286) * (174/286) * (286/2997))
p0 <- ((796/2711) * (1615/2711) * (2711/2997))
p1 / (p1 + p0)

#Naive Bayes probability = ~9.8%
```

Assignment 3 - Part E
Which of the entries in this table are needed for computing P(Loan = 1 | CC = 1, Online = 1)? Run naive Bayes on the data. Examine the model output on training data, and find the entry that corresponds to P(Loan = 1 | CC = 1, Online = 1). Compare this to the number you obtained in (E).
```{r}
#For the first question, the number of entries in the table needed depend on which probability we calculate. If we are calculating the exact probability, we only need 2 entries (49 & 480), but if we are using NB we need all 8 values.

training$Personal.Loan   <- as.factor(training$Personal.Loan)
training$CreditCard     <- as.factor(training$CreditCard)
training$Online <- as.factor(training$Online)

# fitting the model on the training data
nb_model <- naiveBayes(Personal.Loan ~ CreditCard + Online, data = training)

#model output
nb_model

#Examining the model to find the outputs that correspond to P(Loan=1|CC=1,Online=1) and calculate the probability

#P(loan =1) 0.09542876, P(CC=1|Loan=1) 0.2972028, P(Online=1|Loan=1) 0.6083916
#P(loan =0) 0.90457124, P(CC=1|Loan=0) 0.2936186, P(Online=1|Loan=0) 0.5957211
#Now calculate P(Loan = 1 | CC = 1, Online = 1)

PartEProb <- (0.09542876*0.2972028*0.6083916)/((0.09542876*0.2972028*0.6083916)+ (0.90457124*0.2936186*0.5957211))

PartEProb
#This returns the same value obtained in part E of ~9.8%

```
